entities.name: Shapur ibn Sahl
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Shapur ibn Sahl, who died on November 30, 869 CE, was a highly influential Persian physician and pharmacologist active in 9th-century Baghdad, a pivotal center of Islamic Golden Age scholarship. His contributions to medical literature and pharmaceutical practice established him as a landmark figure in the Classical era, particularly within the Abbasid Caliphate's vibrant intellectual milieu. Working at a time when medical knowledge from Greek, Indian, and Persian traditions was being systematically translated and synthesized, Shapur ibn Sahl's systematic approach to drug formulation and therapeutic application profoundly shaped the trajectory of clinical medicine and pharmacy across the Near East and beyond.

His magnum opus, the *Kitāb al-Qarābādhīn* (Book of Medical Formularies), was one of the earliest and most comprehensive medical formularies in Arabic, comprising over 1,500 recipes for compound drugs and treatments. This monumental work, structured methodically by disease and organ system, provided detailed instructions for preparing medicines, including dosages, administration routes, and indications. As chief physician to the Caliph al-Mutawakkil at the famous Hospital of Jundishapur and later in Baghdad, Shapur applied these principles in clinical practice, elevating the standards of patient care and pharmaceutical preparation, and influencing generations of practitioners through his didactic texts.
